title: Rates and causes of death after release from incarceration among 1 471 526 people in eight high-income and middle-income countries: An individual participant data meta-analysis

claims.statement: In people released from prison or jail in eight mostly high-income countries between 1980 and 2018, the death rate was highest in the first week after release, and deaths coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning had the highest rate of any cause in that week, although most such deaths happened later. In 18 record-linkage cohorts of everyone released (1,471,526 people, 88.3% of them men, in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA; 75,427 deaths), the pooled crude death rate was 1,612 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 1,048 to 2,287) in days 2 to 7 after release, against 725 (625 to 831) over the whole follow-up and 737 (636 to 844) more than a year after release; the first week's rate was 1.5 times that of the second week (1.2 to 1.8), 2.0 times that of weeks 3–4 (1.5 to 2.6) and 2.2 times that of weeks 9–12 (1.6 to 3.0). The 'first week' starts on day 2 because in some cohorts deaths in custody had been recorded as deaths on the day of release, which inflated the release-day rate (4,036 per 100,000 person-years, falling to 826 in the ten cohorts that could separate the two). Deaths whose underlying cause was coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning, of unintentional or undetermined intent, a single category that does not separate alcohol, other drugs or combinations and names no drug, had a rate of 657 (332 to 1,076) in days 2 to 7, above suicide (135) and heart and blood vessel disease (71), and of 146 (103 to 197) over the whole follow-up, where they were the leading cause (16,126 deaths, 21.4%); yet 14,671 of these 16,126 deaths (91.0%) happened more than 4 weeks after release (Borschmann et al., 2024), since most of the time people were followed lies beyond the first weeks (the editors' explanation). The study compared periods after release with one another, not with the general population; rates differed greatly between cohorts (236 to 1,183 per 100,000 person-years over the whole follow-up) and regions (days 2 to 7: Europe 2,762, the USA 934); causes came from death registers whose certification and coding were not checked across countries and decades; and it recorded nothing about drug use, treatment in custody or tolerance, so it cannot show why deaths cluster soon after release. Whether, and how fast, tolerance falls during a break from opioids is a separate answer, which rests on reviews (see the answer on tolerance after a break from opioids). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Borschmann et al. (2024), pooled crude rates per 100,000 person-years: all causes, days 2–7 1612 (95% CI 1048–2287), I² 91.1%; whole follow-up 725 (625–831); more than 1 year 737 (636–844); first week vs week 2 IRR 1.5 (1.2–1.8), vs weeks 3–4 2.0 (1.5–2.6), vs weeks 9–12 2.2 (1.6–3.0). Days 2–7 by cause: alcohol and other drug poisoning 657 (332–1076), suicide 135 (36–277), cardiovascular disease 71 (16–153). Whole follow-up: poisoning 146 (103–197), 16,126 of 75,427 deaths (21.4%); 14,671 of the 16,126 (91.0%) more than 4 weeks after release. Release day 4036 (887–8940), 826 (0–3455) in the ten cohorts that separated deaths in custody. Cohorts 236 to 1183; days 2–7 Europe 2762 (1832–3872), USA 934 (389–1703). Excluding time back in custody (16 cohorts) 720 (605–845).
